messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Police Officer
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 65

**Patient Vignette: "Aisha"**

Aisha is a 35-year-old married woman of African descent, a police officer with ten years on the force. She presents for therapy at the urging of her husband, who has grown increasingly worried about her. She has dark circles under her eyes, and her uniform seems to hang on her, as if she has lost weight she didn’t have to lose. She sits forward on the couch, her back ramrod straight, her eyes scanning the room before settling on a fixed point on the wall.

The story begins eighteen months ago, on a night shift that started like any other. Aisha and her partner responded to a domestic disturbance call in a low-income housing complex. The call was routine. The scene was chaotic, with a woman screaming and a man shouting. Aisha’s partner, a man she had trusted for years, told her to secure the hallway while he spoke to the couple. She remembers the smell of stale cooking oil and bleach. She remembers the flickering fluorescent light.

She doesn’t remember the blow to the back of her head. She only remembers waking up on the concrete floor of a basement storage room, her hands cuffed behind her back. Her service weapon was gone. Her partner, the man who had told her to secure the hallway, was standing over her. He was not the man she worked with. He was a stranger with a cold, calm voice. He told her she was a "bitch who thought she was better than the men" and that he was going to "teach her a lesson." The assault was brutal, methodical, and silent. He did not speak again. When he was finished, he uncuffed her, told her to get dressed, and said that if she told anyone, he would say she attacked him first. He would say she was hysterical, that he had to restrain her. He would say it was consensual. He left her there, on the concrete, in the dark.

Aisha did not tell anyone. She went home, showered until the water ran cold, and went to work the next day. She told herself it was a nightmare. She told herself she had to be strong. She was a cop. Cops don't get assaulted. Cops handle things.

In the months that followed, Aisha’s world began to shrink. At work, she became hypervigilant. She can no longer ride in a squad car with a male partner without her heart pounding so hard she feels she might vomit. She insists on driving, and she keeps her hand on her baton. She avoids the locker room. She has stopped going to the shooting range, because the sound of a gunshot—any gunshot—sends her into a cold sweat. She has been written up twice for insubordination after snapping at a male sergeant who touched her shoulder to get her attention. She feels a constant, low-grade rage that she has to choke down.

At home, the rage turns to numbness. She has stopped sleeping in the same bed as her husband. She cannot bear to be touched, even a gentle hand on her back. She lies on the floor of the living room, fully clothed, with all the lights on, listening for footsteps. She has nightmares, but she doesn’t remember them. She only wakes up gasping, with the smell of bleach in her nose. She has stopped cooking, stopped laughing. Her husband has stopped asking what is wrong. He just looks at her with a kind of sad, tired fear.

The trigger that finally brought her here was a routine traffic stop. A man in a pickup truck had a broken taillight. When Aisha approached the driver’s side window, the man was speaking on his phone. He was a large man, with a deep voice. He did not look at her. He just held up a finger, telling her to wait. For a split second, she was back in that basement. She felt the concrete under her cheek. She saw the flickering light. She unholstered her weapon and pointed it at the man’s head. She screamed for him to get out of the car. He dropped the phone, his face white. She was shaking so badly she could barely hold the gun. Her backup arrived, and they had to physically lower her arm. She was put on administrative leave.

Now, she sits in my office. Her hands are clasped tightly in her lap. She is a police officer who no longer trusts her own judgment. She is a wife who cannot be touched. She is a survivor who feels like a coward. She tells me, her voice flat, that she is fine. She just needs to get back on the horse. She just needs to forget. She looks at me, and for a moment, the mask slips. I see the terror of a woman trapped in a basement, waiting for a door to open that she knows she cannot lock.
